5SI ENGLISH  ·  POINT OF VIEW
Unit 1 · Week 2 · Lesson 9
L9 The skill first. Two texts to apply it to.

Whose Story
Is This?

Every story is told by someone. Point of view is the choice of who that someone is, and it decides what we see, what we know, and whose side we are on. Today we learn to spot it, name it, and understand what it does.

👁
The move: find the narrator → name the point of view → explain what it lets the reader know.
1 Learning objective

To identify a text’s point of view, and explain how the choice of narrator shapes what the reader knows.

Success criteria

  • I can find the narrator by reading outside the speech marks.
  • I can tell first person from third person, using the signal words.
  • I can explain what each point of view lets the reader know, and hides.
  • I can retell a moment from a different narrator’s point of view.

The trap to avoid

A character saying “I” inside dialogue does not make the story first person. The narrator is the voice outside the speech marks. Ignore the quotes and read the narration.

You will meet a third-person folktale and a first-person story, and read both like a detective.

2 The big idea

Someone is always telling the story. Who?

First person

“I knocked on the door.”

The narrator is in the story.

vs
Third person

“He knocked on the door.”

The narrator stands outside it.

Same door, same knock. The only difference is the pronoun in the narration, and that single choice changes whose eyes we borrow for the whole story.

Starter · Quick fire

First or third? Point to the signal word.

“We lay down the hardboard and cranked up the volume.”

First person · “we”.

“Velvel worried each night about how to survive.”

Third person · “Velvel”, “he”.

“I staked out a spot near the underground.”

First person · “I”.

“The servant ushered him inside and brushed the dust from his clothes.”

Third person · “him”, “his”.

Starter · The trap

There is an “I” here. So is it first person?

“I am Velvel of Dolna, a poor village far away,” he said to the servant.

No. The “I” sits inside the speech marks, so it belongs to a character talking. The narration, “he said”, is third person. Always read outside the quotes to decide.

Starter · Whose eyes?

One handshake, told three ways.

Velvel (first)

“I shook his hand, hiding my grin.”

We know the trick.

Feldman (first)

“I paid gladly, sure I had bought something precious.”

We share his hope, not the trick.

Outside (third)

“The two men shook hands over the tea.”

We watch, and judge for ourselves.

💡
Same facts, three different stories. Point of view decides what we know and how we feel.
Starter · What can they know?

A first-person narrator describes a party. What can they truthfully tell you?

What they themselves felt

Yes.

What they watched a friend do

Yes.

What a stranger across the room was secretly thinking

No, they cannot see inside another head.

🔒
First person is locked inside one mind. That limit is exactly what makes it feel close, and what it cannot show.
Lens · How to find it

The narrator lives outside the speech marks.

Two steps

1

Cover the dialogue. Read only the narration.

2

Find the signal words: the pronouns the narration uses.

Signal words

First person: I, me, my, we, us, our.

Third person: he, she, they, him, her, and the characters’ names.

This is the “box the signal words” step on the worksheet.

Template · The two voices

First person or third person

First person
Pronouns I, we, my, our
Narrator a character, inside the story
We access one person’s thoughts and feelings
Feel close, personal, easy to trust or doubt
Third person
Pronouns he, she, they, names
Narrator an observer, outside the story
We access the outside, and sometimes several minds
Feel wider, more distant, freer to judge
Lens · The trade-off

Every point of view gains something and loses something.

First person buys intimacy

We live inside one head. We feel what they feel and know only what they know. The cost: a single, possibly biased, view.

Third person buys overview

The narrator can step back, follow more than one person, and let the reader see what characters miss. The cost: less closeness.

⚠
Trust test: a first-person narrator can be wrong, biased, or hiding something. Ask what they might not be telling you.
Template · Prove and explain

Name it. Prove it. Explain the effect.

Evidence

“our overload of energy”

A signal word from the narration.

→
Point of view

First person: “our” puts the narrator inside the crew.

→
Effect

We share the crew’s experience from the inside, so we root for them.

The story is told in person. The word “” shows this, which makes the reader .

Template · Change the storyteller

To retell from a new narrator

1

Swap the pronouns. He becomes I, or I becomes he.

2

Swap the knowledge. Tell only what the new narrator can see, know and feel. Cut what they could not know; add their private thoughts.

3

Keep the events the same. Same facts, new eyes.

✎
“He nervously knocked” → from Velvel: “My hand shook as I knocked.” From Feldman inside: he never sees the nerves at all, only “a ragged man at the door”.
I do · Modelled

Watch me work one line.

“The servant ushered Velvel inside and brushed the dust from his clothes.”

Find

Pure narration, no dialogue. Signal words: “Velvel”, “his”.

Name

Third person.

Effect

We watch from outside, kindly but distant, so Velvel’s hidden plan stays hidden and the twist can land.

We do · Together on the board

Your turn to drive.

“My b-boy crew began working on dance moves to deal with our overload of energy.”

Model: first person (“my”, “our”). We are inside the crew, sharing their drive, so their success feels like ours.

“‘Come live in Dolna,’ Velvel replied, ‘where no rich man has ever died!’”

Model: careful. All of this is dialogue. The narration around it, “Velvel replied”, is third person. The trap again.

You do · Pairs

Detective. Name it, prove it, mind the trap.

“We wore matching T-shirts and struck our starting pose.”

First · “we”, “our”.

“Without hesitation, Mr Feldman counted out the money.”

Third · “Mr Feldman”.

“‘I’m willing to sell you the secret of eternal life,’ he said.”

Third · “he said”. The “I” is dialogue. Trap.

💬
Task: for each, agree first or third, then point to the exact signal word outside the quotes.
You do · Stretch

Same moment, new eyes.

Third person: “He nervously knocked on the door, then straightened his ragged coat.”

Retell as Velvel (first person). Change the pronouns, and add what he is really thinking as he knocks.

Then retell as Feldman inside the house. He cannot see the nerves. What does his version leave out?

💡
Notice how much the reader learns changes with the narrator. That is the whole point of point of view.
3 Now apply it · Text 1

The Bargain · a third-person folktale

Watch for

The narrator stands outside and follows Velvel. We never hear his plan, so the ending surprises us. This text is full of “I” inside dialogue. Do not be fooled: check the narration.

Full text on the worksheet, coming up.

Bring your tools

Box the signal words. Read outside the quotes. Name the person. Then ask: what does this distance let the writer hide until the last line?

3 Now apply it · Text 2

Becoming B-boys · a first-person story

Watch for

“My crew”, “we”, “I staked out a spot”. We are inside one dancer. We meet Cato only through the narrator’s admiring eyes, and know only what the narrator knows.

Bring your tools

Box the signal words. Name the person. Then ask the key question: why did the writer choose first person here? What does being inside the crew give the reader?

4 Worksheets

You’ve got the skill.
Now apply it.

Annotate on the sheets, answer the questions in your notebook. Read outside the speech marks, box the signal words, and explain the effect.

Check as you write: precise evidence → point of view → explained inference. Point to a signal word, do not just assert the person.

5 Exit ticket

Any story you know well.

Name its point of view, point to one signal word, and explain one thing that narrator cannot tell you.

Read outside the speech marks. Prove it with a signal word. The move you own now.
